description: Blissfall is a six-member team from Beirut tackling NASA’s Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. We bring together software engineering, data visualization, 3D graphics, and space-science backgrounds, driven by curiosity about the Moon’s south pole and what it takes to land there safely. Expect something ambitious at Space Apps 2026 — details coming at the event.
summary:
Team Blissfall's SiteLine is a 3D web app created to solve the challenge of NASA Space Apps 2026: Lunar Landing Site Navigator. It can help answer the question of missions such as Artemis IV: When and where would it be safe to land close to the south pole of the Moon?
You come down from the solar system to the Moon, click anywhere and see your Pass/fail. Siteline examines four parameters: sunlight, direct line of sight to Earth, landing slope, distance from the pole. It also displays the distance to the nearest ice and why a site is failing.
You will be able to compare up to 4 sites, read a site against a particular robot's requirements, preview the landing, and walk the surface at real scale. The in-built AI voice guide Luna will tell you the results and guide you there.
All numbers are from NASA data, shown in the source column. Mars is included as well.

details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

SiteLine is a 3D web app for choosing a landing site near the Moon’s south pole. You fly from the solar system down to the pole, click any spot and pick a date. SiteLine then tells you whether the spot passes for the whole stay: whether the Sun stays above the real horizon for power, whether Earth stays in view for radio contact, whether the ground is flat enough and whether the spot lies in an Artemis region. It also shows the nearest cold trap where ice could survive, and a slider re-checks everything if the launch slips. Each horizon is calculated from NASA’s LOLA terrain, and the positions of the Sun and Earth come from NASA’s SPICE toolkit. You can also search for sites that pass, compare up to four, check whether a rover or lander fits, walk a spot in first person as an astronaut, and ask our AI guide, Luna, to do any of this by voice or text.

What benefits does it have?

SiteLine puts power, communications, terrain and schedule risk side by side in seconds, for any spot and date. Because it uses the real horizon rather than a flat one, its sunlight results agree with NASA’s own illumination maps to within one percentage point at published test points. Every number shows its source, unknowns are never shown as passes, and it runs in any browser with plain-language explanations.

What is the intended impact?

We want lunar site selection to be something students, the public and early mission teams can explore and understand: why the south pole is so valuable, why it is so difficult, and how a short launch delay can turn a good site into a bad one. SiteLine is a screening aid, not a mission certification tool.

What tools did you use?

We wrote the app in TypeScript, with React, three.js and Vite, and the data pipeline in Python. The data comes from NASA SPICE, LRO LOLA terrain, the Artemis III terrain models, NASA’s illumination maps, MOLA for Mars and NASA 3D models. The site is hosted on Cloudflare Pages and R2. Luna runs on Cloudflare Workers AI, and her voice runs on LiveKit, Deepgram and Cartesia. We used Blender for the astronaut model and Vitest and Playwright for testing. Claude Code helped us develop, with every change reviewed by a person. Everything was built on ordinary laptops, and the app runs on any modern device.

How is it creative?

SiteLine is one continuous journey, from the whole solar system down to standing on the spot where you would land. A pass or fail becomes something you can walk through and see. The launch slider makes schedule risk visible, and Luna moves the view and runs the checks for you while only repeating numbers SiteLine itself calculated.

What factors did the team consider?

We considered scientific accuracy (NASA’s reference frames, careful time scales and the real horizon), data integrity (no invented data, and every dataset credited), and honesty about limits. We also considered accessibility (icons and words, never colour alone, plus keyboard support), performance on laptops, phones and slow connections, low cost, and teamwork across six roles with reviewed changes and automated tests.
